transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-03
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/records/ff-20260903-td-8392 (internal)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood Solutions); Ravi Patel (CTO, Tangent AI), Sofia Gomez (Head of Platform), Evan Lee (ML Engineer), Marta Ruiz (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may contain errors): p95 and token throughput requirements; need Dedicated for predictable bursts; Private for data residency maybe; run tests.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood. Quick audio check?
[00:06] Ravi: Audio good, thanks Maya.
[00:12] Liam: Hi team, Liam here, I'm going to cover the performance / benchmarking stuff later in the call.
[00:18] Sofia: Great, we just want to make sure we cover our SLOs and networking constraints upfront.
[00:25] Maya: Perfect. Intent for this call is discovery — understand your p95 targets, concurrency patterns, whether you need Hosted, Dedicated, or Private. Also collect prompt set for a benchmark.

[01:05] Ravi: High level -- Tangent's product does live conversational summaries for telehealth sessions. Short responses mostly, lots of streaming for transcripts. Our target p95 for the end-to-end generation step is 250-300ms for <60 token responses. For longer summaries (200-600 tokens) we can tolerate 1.2-1.5s p95. Burst pattern: we expect spikes when groups of sessions end, roughly 600-900 concurrent short streams during peak times.

[01:48] Evan: To add, our sequence lengths are usually short for realtime suggestions, but sometimes we request full-note generation which is the long tail. We use prefix caching on some requests now in-house.

[02:15] Liam: Okay, that's helpful. Quick clarifying q: when you say 600-900 concurrent, is that full token-streaming pipes or just concurrent inference requests?
[02:26] Ravi: It's active WebSocket streams; each stream sends tokens on the fly and expects server-sent events. So it's streaming, not single-shot.

[02:38] Priya: Noted. That pushes on how we do batching and KV cache management. Streaming with thousands of open connections can be a diff profile than burst single-shot qps.

[03:04] Marta: Security wise we need SOC2, audit logs, and KMS support. Private deployment is preferred if Redwood can't guarantee audit-level logs in Hosted. Also SSO via SAML.

[03:25] Maya: Redwood supports SOC2 and we have KMS integrations for Dedicated and Private. Hosted also supports KMS for BYOK in some setups, but for strict audit logs Private gives you the most control. We'll share the security deck.

[03:52] Sofia: Ideal procurement timeline is to have a pilot in Oct and production by Q4. Procurement requires all security docs and a pilot cost estimate.

[04:15] Liam: Let's dig into latency. For short responses, p95 250ms is tight but achievable depending on model and batching. Are you using a smaller open model or a larger one?
[04:28] Evan: We're experimenting with a mix: base open models for short replies, and a heavier 7B-ish model for summaries. We might quantize. We care about hallucination rates too but that's lower priority for this call.

[04:50] Liam: For 7B we can typically hit ~200-300ms p95 on Dedicated with optimized runtime for short sequences with continuous KV caching and small batch windows; Hosted performance varies with tenancy and request routing.

[05:12] Ravi: Can you explain the routing? If we start on Hosted and then move to Dedicated, how seamless is it?
[05:21] Maya: The API is the same. You can pin models and rollout policies. For routing, we do smart routing by latency policy and region. You can also configure fallback to smaller quantized variants if Dedicated capacity is saturated.

[05:41] Evan: About caching - we do prefix reuse for certain prompts. How does Redwood handle prefix/KV caching in streaming? Does it keep KV per session?
[05:54] Liam: We maintain per-connection KV caches in the runtime; when you have streaming sessions that reuse similar prefixes we can reuse cached states which reduces token compute significantly. Watch out for memory pressure at large concurrency—eviction policy is LRU by default.

[06:22] Sofia: For networking — Private/VPC works well for us. We need to ensure we can connect from our EKS clusters into Redwood VPC endpoints and have full audit logging available.

[06:35] Maya: Noted. We'll include a VPC wiring diagram and typical firewall rules.

[07:00] Liam: On throughput—token/sec is a useful metric. For short tokens (say 3 tokens per response), bursts of 900 concurrent streams at 2 tokens/sec each is ~5400 tokens/sec sustained during peaks. With batching and KV reuse, the per-token cost drops. But the runtime scheduling matters: continuous batching gives us better GPU utilization but impacts tail latency if you increase the batch window.

[07:36] Ravi: So what's the trade-off — if you configure lower batch windows we get better p95 but waste GPU?
[07:44] Liam: Exactly. There's a latency vs cost tradeoff. On Dedicated you can tune batch windows and burst autoscaling so you have both predictable latency and cost controls. On Hosted the runtime chooses defaults to balance across tenants.

[08:05] Evan: Could you give a concrete example for 7B model: p95 numbers at different batch strategies?
[08:13] Liam: Sure, ballpark: Dedicated optimized runtime with batch window 10ms, small prefix lengths — p95 about 180-260ms for short replies. Increase batch window to 50ms to improve throughput and reduce cost per token, p95 might increase to 300-450ms. If you enable quantized int8 paths you can shave tokens/sec cost but sometimes add a small latency penalty on first token.

[08:46] Priya: And burst scaling — do you have instant warm pools? We can't afford long cold starts during user-critical spikes.

[08:55] Maya: Dedicated has options for reserved warm pools and burst capacity; you can configure steady state + burst. We'll include the SLA for cold starts but generally warm pools avoid cold VM/GPU attach times.

[09:14] Marta: For audit logs we need per-request tracing and token-level usage logs for compliance. Is that available?

[09:22] Liam: Yes, we provide per-request traces via the Console. Token-level cost and latency breakdowns are available. For Private deployments we can forward logs to your SIEM. In Hosted we provide an exportable audit log too.

[09:45] Sofia: Pricing — rough numbers for Dedicated vs Hosted for our expected load?

[09:52] Maya: We'll share a tailored pricing sheet after we run a benchmark, but rough guidance: Hosted is pay-as-you-go with per-token pricing; Dedicated is reserved capacity with lower unit cost but commit. For bursty workloads, Dedicated with burst credits often ends up cheaper for intense peaks.

[10:18] Evan: Could you detail the benchmark you propose? We want to see p95 for short streaming, sustained tokens/sec, and behavior during a 10-minute ramp to peak.

[10:28] Liam: Proposed benchmark: 1) Short-stream test: 1k short prompts (avg 8 tokens) across streaming connections ramp to 900 concurrent over 10 minutes, measure p50/p95/p99 for first-token and full response. 2) Sustained token test: run a 30-minute sustained tokens/sec at expected peak. 3) Cold-start probe: scale from 0 to peak to measure warmup times. We'll run these on Hosted and Dedicated (if you approve Dedicated test). We'll also include a quantized model run.

[11:05] Ravi: We want the CSV results and a spreadsheet with cost calc assuming our token distributions.

[11:11] Maya: We'll deliver CSVs and a breakdown in the benchmark doc. Liam will run the harness.

[11:26] Priya: Any caveats about WebSocket connection limits per host? We run in multiple AZs with ingress LB.

[11:36] Liam: There are connection limits at the LB and runtime layer. For Dedicated we can provision more frontends and scale the connection handling. We'll document recommended fronting patterns.

[12:01] Evan: Regarding model variants — we'd like automatic fallback to smaller models during congestion. Can Redwood do automatic model variant fallback based on latency?

[12:11] Maya: Yes, you can define rollout/fallback policies: fallback to a compatible, lower-cost variant when latency or capacity thresholds are breached. That does change semantics slightly so you'll want to test evals.

[12:36] Marta: When fallback happens, do logs show which model served each request? We need traceability.
[12:42] Liam: Yes, per-request metadata includes model id, variant, and route used.

[12:55] Ravi: Are there any examples where Dedicated couldn't satisfy sub-300ms p95?
[13:02] Liam: If you use very large models (20B+) or extremely long sequences, it gets challenging. But for 7B-ish ranges with good quantization and caching, Dedicated can be tuned to meet 250-300ms p95 for short responses. Also network latency from your clients matters — we measure from Redwood edge to runtime, not client-to-edge.

[13:29] Sofia: On client side network --- our users sometimes sit on mobile with 100-200ms of additional latency. So we need some buffer in server p95.

[13:41] Maya: Understood. We'll present p95 breakdowns by stage (edge, runtime, tokenization).

[14:02] Evan: For the benchmark, can we include one test with our real transcripts so prefix reuse kicks in?

[14:10] Liam: Absolutely. That's why Evan should upload those prompts. Prefix reuse will show big wins in tokens/sec and p95.

[14:35] Ravi: What's the expected memory footprint for per-session KV caches at 900 concurrent? Rough numbers?

[14:42] Liam: Roughly, per-session KV depends on sequence length and model size; ballpark 5-20MB per session for active caches on 7B. Multiply by 900 and that's several GBs — runtime keeps this in GPU host memory; Dedicated nodes are sized accordingly. We can provide exact numbers after we know average prefixes.

[15:07] Priya: So if we use Dedicated with 4 GPU nodes, would that be enough?

[15:14] Liam: Might be; depends on model quantization, batch sizes, and token rates. The benchmark will tell. We also have autoscaling to burst beyond baseline.

[15:34] Sofia: Let's touch on Private — we might need an on-prem option for certain customers in healthcare. How heavy is the install?

[15:42] Maya: Private on-prem is an appliance-like deploy with our control plane optionally air-gapped. It requires Kubernetes orchestration and recommended GPU infra. We provide an install guide and SRE support. For strict regulated customers it's common.

[16:05] Marta: KMS integration in Private — can we plug into our HSM?

[16:11] Liam: Yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM. We'll include an integration checklist.

[16:32] Evan: A couple of practical asks: can you provide expected token/sec per GPU for the 7B model on your quantized path? Even rough numbers help us capacity plan.

[16:42] Liam: Rough: 7B int8 optimized path can do ~20k-40k tokens/sec per GPU under ideal short-token workloads with batching and KV reuse. Without reuse, numbers drop. We'll include these in the benchmark doc with measured values.

[17:05] Ravi: Will you include p99 and p95 so we can see tail behavior? p99 is important for UX.

[17:12] Liam: Yes p50/p95/p99 and histograms. Also first-token vs streaming tail latencies.

[17:34] Priya: Does Redwood provide SDKs for streaming that handle reconnect/resume and token deltas?

[17:42] Maya: Yes, SDKs for Node/Python with reconnect helpers and partial delta heuristics. We'll link the SDK repo; note some client-side behavior may need adjustment when you do fallback.

[18:03] Evan: Any gotchas with websocket keepalive? We had some issues with certain load balancers dropping long-lived connections.

[18:12] Liam: We recommend using ALBs with long keepalive settings or sticky frontends; for Dedicated we can provision connection frontends in each AZ. We'll give config examples.

[18:39] Sofia: For procurement, what legal documents do you need — standard MSA, DPA?

[18:46] Maya: Standard MSA and DPA, plus any BAA if needed for healthcare. We'll send templates.

[19:02] Marta: Can you support per-tenant rate limits and quotas within Dedicated? We want to isolate internal services.

[19:10] Liam: Yes, we have token-level quotas and route-based policies. Dedicated gives you more control.

[19:28] Ravi: Let's talk timelines. If we approve a pilot next week, how quickly can Redwood spin up a Dedicated pilot and run the benchmarks?

[19:38] Maya: Dedicated pilot provisioning is typically 2-3 weeks depending on capacity and set up. Hosted benchmark can start within 48 hours. Private takes longer — usually 6-8 weeks.

[20:01] Evan: Is there a minimum for Dedicated? Like commit or term?

[20:07] Maya: For Dedicated there's a minimum monthly commit; we'll include options for short pilots with elevated per-unit pricing vs standard reserved rates. Pilot pricing details in the follow-up.

[20:25] Priya: For the data flows, do you persist requests in Hosted? We need retention controls.

[20:32] Liam: By default Hosted retains logs short-term but you can configure retention and data deletion policies; Dedicated and Private give you finer control. We'll send retention matrix.

[20:56] Evan: Anything else on fallback semantics — if a request is downgraded mid-stream, how do you surface that?

[21:04] Liam: We expose model id on every token event so you can see which variant produced which chunk. For mid-stream fallback we provide a header/event indicating fallback triggered. We recommend testing for discontinuities in evals.

[21:32] Maya: Quick pause to recap the test plan and owners. Liam will run the benchmark; Maya sends pricing and security docs; Evan uploads prompts; Sofia confirms procurement timeline; Marta verifies security checklist.

[21:50] Ravi: Sounds good. A couple of quick Qs: do you have pre-built dashboards for token-level cost by route?

[21:59] Liam: Yes, Console has route/model dashboards and can break down token costs at token granularity (sampled). We'll provide screenshots.

[22:20] Priya: Can we get a short demo of the Console during the pilot?

[22:27] Maya: Absolutely, we'll schedule a 30-minute Console walkthrough post-benchmark.

[22:40] Evan: On the security deck — include SOC2 scope and whether any of the storage is outside region (we have EU data residency reqs).

[22:50] Marta: Also need details for audit log retention and SIEM forwarding specifics.

[23:04] Maya: We'll include region/residency info and SIEM forwarding options.

[23:20] Liam: Just to call out one important technical note — streaming p95 includes both network to the edge and edge to runtime. If you need <300ms p95 end-to-end, keep edge region close to your users or use multi-region fronting.

[23:42] Ravi: We'll provide geographic distribution of our users to help pick regions.

[24:00] Evan: For the CSV output, include per-request metadata: model_id, variant, p50/p95/p99, tokens, GPU used.

[24:10] Liam: Yep, that's the plan.

[24:22] Priya: Any limitations for K8s ingress patterns we should follow?

[24:31] Liam: Use HTTP/2 or WebSocket support, sticky session patterns recommended; keep alive tuned. We'll send examples.

[24:54] Maya: I'll read back next steps now. Redwood to: 1) Kick off Hosted benchmark in 48h after we receive prompts; 2) Share Dedicated pilot pricing and warm-pool options; 3) Share security artifact bundle (SOC2, KMS/HSM integrations, DPA/MSA). Tangent to: 1) Upload prompts and traffic shape, 2) Confirm procurement timeline and VPC requirement.

[25:27] Ravi: Good. Also please include estimated tokens/sec per GPU in the doc.

[25:34] Liam: We'll include measured tokens/sec on each run (Hosted and Dedicated) and a scaled estimate for capacity planning.

[25:50] Maya: Any final concerns from Tangent?

[25:55] Sofia: Main concern is predictable tail latency during bursts and ensuring audits.

[26:00] Marta: And KMS/HSM integration details.

[26:06] Maya: Great. We'll follow up with the benchmark plan and calendar invites.

[26:15] Evan: One small nit — when you say "quantized path" can you confirm if your runtime uses per-channel quantization or whole-tensor? We've seen quality regressions on some models.

[26:24] Liam: We support a couple quantization strategies, including per-channel 8-bit quant on certain weights; we'll include which strategies we used in the quant runs. You'll be able to compare quality vs latency.

[26:44] Ravi: Can we get a short example of how the fallback policy is defined (JSON or config)?

[26:50] Priya: Yeah show us a fallback that says: if p95 > 400ms for >5m, route X -> model Y.
[26:57] Maya: We'll include sample rollout and fallback policy configs in the follow-up.

[27:10] Evan: Okay that's it from our side for now.

[27:15] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll send the follow-ups and the benchmark kickoff link.

[27:22] Ravi: Appreciate it.

[27:28] -- end of recorded discussion --
